approaches.name: Direct anterior approach to the hip (periprosthetic)
approaches.corridor: Anterior Hueter interval between tensor fasciae latae (superior gluteal nerve) and sartorius/rectus femoris (femoral nerve), through a T-capsulotomy to the femoral head and neck

procedure_applications.condition: Total hip arthroplasty is performed through an anterior intermuscular interval
An anterior exposure that preserves the posterior capsule is preferred for a periprosthetic fracture

positioning.text: Position supine on a standard or specialty table with the ipsilateral arm padded across the chest and the limb free for traction and rotation.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the anterior superior iliac spine and the tensor fasciae latae; the incision runs from just lateral and distal to the ASIS toward the lateral femoral epicondyle over the TFL.

incision.text: Make an approximately 10 cm incision over the tensor fasciae latae, entering the TFL sheath from its medial side to spare the muscle belly.

superficial_interval.text: Develop the Hueter interval between the tensor fasciae latae laterally and the sartorius and rectus femoris medially, keeping the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve protected within the sartorial fascia.

deep_interval.text: Isolate and coagulate the ascending branch of the lateral femoral circumflex vessels, place a retractor around the superior femoral neck, and expose the anterior capsule.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue with the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, TFL sheath, the intermuscular Hueter interval, the lateral femoral circumflex vessels, and the anterior hip capsule.

structures_at_risk.text: The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, the femoral nerve deep to an aggressive medial retractor, and the ascending branch of the lateral femoral circumflex artery are at risk.

danger_zones.text: The medial edge of the interval is the danger zone: branches of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve that perforate the fascia early, and femoral nerve traction from a deep medial retractor.

retraction_hazards.text: Avoid forceful medial retraction, which can injure the femoral nerve, and protect lateral femoral cutaneous nerve branches in the subcutaneous fat.

exposure.text: A T-shaped capsulotomy with medial and lateral stay sutures exposes the femoral head and neck for arthroplasty or fracture work.

limitations.text: The approach gives restricted access to posterior wall and column fractures and limited femoral exposure without extension.

indications.text: Indicated for primary total hip arthroplasty and for periprosthetic fracture treatment where the posterior capsule is preserved, and it can be extended for fixation.

closure.text: Close the capsule with non-absorbable sutures, close the TFL fascia, and consider a subfascial drain given the bleeding risk from the circumflex vessels.

complications.text: Complications include lateral femoral cutaneous nerve paresthesia, femoral nerve injury, wound problems, and bleeding from the lateral femoral circumflex vessels.

questions.question: Which intermuscular interval defines the direct anterior approach?
questions.answer: The Hueter interval between tensor fasciae latae and sartorius/rectus femoris.

questions.question: Which cutaneous nerve is characteristically injured in the direct anterior approach?
Which vessels are coagulated during the deep dissection?
questions.answer: The ascending branch of the lateral femoral circumflex vessels.

approaches.name: Direct lateral (Hardinge) approach to the proximal femur (periprosthetic)
approaches.corridor: Transgluteal split of gluteus medius and vastus lateralis raising an anterior myofascial sleeve to reach the anterior hip capsule and proximal femur

sources.title: Direct lateral approach to the proximal femur (periprosthetic hip)

procedure_applications.condition: A periprosthetic proximal femoral fracture needs lateral exposure of the hip and femur
Hemiarthroplasty is performed through a direct lateral exposure

positioning.text: Position in lateral decubitus or supine with the greater trochanter accessible and the limb free.

surface_landmarks.text: Center the incision over the greater trochanter with its proximal end directed slightly posteriorly.

incision.text: Make a longitudinal incision through skin and subcutaneous tissue down to the fascia lata over the trochanter.

superficial_interval.text: Split the fascia lata and release the anterior third of gluteus medius and minimus while preserving their posterior femoral attachment.

deep_interval.text: Elevate the anterior fibers of vastus lateralis from the anterior femur in continuity with the abductors to create an anterior myofascial sleeve, then perform an anterior longitudinal capsulotomy with a proximal transverse limb.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, fascia lata, gluteus medius and minimus anteriorly, vastus lateralis, and the anterior hip capsule.

structures_at_risk.text: The superior gluteal nerve, which crosses 3 to 5 cm proximal to the tip of the greater trochanter, limits proximal splitting of the abductors and its injury causes abductor weakness.

danger_zones.text: Splitting the gluteus medius more than 3 to 5 cm above the trochanteric tip is the danger zone for the superior gluteal nerve.

retraction_hazards.text: Do not extend the abductor split proximally beyond the safe margin and avoid excessive proximal retraction on the medius.

exposure.text: Gentle external rotation, and dislocation if needed, exposes the femoral head, neck, and proximal femur.

limitations.text: Violation of the abductor mechanism can cause a postoperative limp, and heterotopic ossification is common.

indications.text: Excellent for periprosthetic fractures of the proximal femur and usable for revision arthroplasty and hemiarthroplasty.

closure.text: Reattach the anterior myofascial sleeve securely with heavy sutures, close in layers, and consider a subfascial drain given the blood loss risk.

complications.text: Complications include superior gluteal nerve injury with abductor weakness and limp, heterotopic ossification, and wound problems.

questions.question: How far above the greater trochanter does the superior gluteal nerve cross?
questions.answer: About 3 to 5 cm proximal to the tip of the greater trochanter.

questions.question: What is created by elevating the anterior abductors with vastus lateralis?
What is the characteristic late complication of the direct lateral approach?
questions.answer: Abductor weakness with a postoperative limp.

approaches.name: Posterolateral approach to the hip (periprosthetic)
approaches.corridor: Posterolateral split of gluteus maximus with detachment of the short external rotators and a posterior capsulotomy to reach the posterior hip and femur

procedure_applications.condition: A periprosthetic femoral fracture or revision needs posterior exposure of the hip and femur
Revision hip arthroplasty is performed posteriorly

positioning.text: Position in lateral decubitus with supports preventing rotation away from true lateral and padding at pressure points; prone positioning is also possible.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the posterior superior iliac spine, the greater trochanter, and the femoral shaft.

incision.text: Curve the incision toward the PSIS to a point about 6 cm proximal to the greater trochanter and extend it about 6 cm distally along the femoral axis.

superficial_interval.text: Incise the fascia lata and split the gluteus maximus in line with its fibers across the greater trochanter.

deep_interval.text: Place heavy stay sutures in the piriformis and conjoined obturator internus and gemelli, detach the short external rotators bluntly, and open a broad-based three-sided posterior capsulotomy.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, fascia lata, gluteus maximus, the short external rotators, and the posterior hip capsule.

structures_at_risk.text: The sciatic nerve lies just posterior to the short external rotators and must be protected, and its exposure is unnecessary for routine arthroplasty.

danger_zones.text: The interval deep to the short external rotators and quadratus femoris is the danger zone for the sciatic nerve.

retraction_hazards.text: Keep the hip extended and knee flexed and avoid deep posterior retraction that stretches the sciatic nerve.

exposure.text: Exposes the posterior hip, femoral head and neck, and proximal femur for arthroplasty or fracture fixation.

limitations.text: The posterior approach has a higher dislocation rate than anterior exposures unless the capsule and rotators are securely repaired.

indications.text: Indicated for revision hip arthroplasty and open reduction and internal fixation of periprosthetic femoral fractures.

closure.text: Repair the short external rotators and capsule through drill holes in the posterior greater trochanter, since secure repair reduces dislocation, then close in layers with a subfascial drain.

complications.text: Complications include posterior hip dislocation, sciatic nerve injury, and wound problems.

questions.question: Which nerve is most at risk in the posterolateral hip approach?
questions.answer: The sciatic nerve, lying just posterior to the short external rotators.

questions.question: What most reduces dislocation risk after a posterior approach?
questions.answer: Secure repair of the capsule and short external rotators.

questions.question: Which muscle is split to reach the short external rotators?
questions.answer: The gluteus maximus, in line with its fibers.
